summary: We developed LUNA // South Pole Ops, an interactive web-based 3D mission planning simulator built with Three.js and NASA lunar elevation datasets. Featuring a tactical HUD interface, the application allows users to rotate a high-resolution 3D Moon, dynamically adjust solar azimuth and elevation vectors, track real-time surface coordinates via cursor raycasting, and evaluate key lunar sites like Shackleton Crater and Artemis III candidates.   This tool directly addresses the challenge by replacing complex, specialist-only astronomical interfaces with an intuitive visual platform. By simulating extreme low-angle sunlight and real-time shadows across lunar topography, users can immediately assess solar power generation potential and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight communication windows across different dates and landing coordinates.   This is important because missions to the Moon’s south pole operate under razor-thin margins for power survival and signal blackouts. Making this spatial data accessible empowers mission planners to rapidly compare landing sites, while giving educators and the public an engaging, hands-on way to understand the engineering realities of humanity's return to the Moon.
details:
What it does & how it worksLUNA // South Pole Ops is a browser-based 3D simulator built to make lunar mission planning visual and fast. You get an interactive 3D Moon in the center of the screen surrounded by a tactical HUD. You can rotate and zoom around the lunar south pole, hover over the surface to read exact coordinates in real time, and use sliders to change the Sun’s azimuth and elevation. As you move the Sun, the app casts realistic low-angle shadows across the craters so you can immediately see which areas stay lit for solar power and which ones have a clear line of sight back to Earth. We also pinned key mission locations—like Shackleton Crater and Artemis III candidate sites—so you can click and compare them right away.

Tools & tech stack

  • Code: HTML5, CSS3 (Tailwind CSS), and JavaScript.
  • 3D Engine: Three.js (using OrbitControls for camera movement and Raycaster for tracking coordinates on the surface).
  • Data & Textures: NASA’s CGI Moon Kit (SVS) for the lunar surface textures and LRO elevation maps.

Benefits & intended impact Existing tools for checking Sun and Earth positions on the Moon are built for specialists and can be slow to navigate. Our goal was to strip away that complexity so mission planners can compare landing sites in seconds, while giving teachers, students, and space fans an intuitive, hands-on way to see why landing at the lunar south pole is so challenging.

What makes it creative Instead of showing static charts or raw spreadsheets, we took inspiration from tactical video game interfaces and sci-fi control rooms. Mixing game-style HUD elements with real NASA elevation data turns complex orbital lighting into something anyone can explore and understand just by dragging a slider.

Key factors we considered

  • Smooth performance: Rendering heavy 3D lunar terrain can easily lag a browser, so we used lightweight Three.js spheres and optimized texture maps to keep it running smoothly on standard laptops.
  • Clarity on one screen: We designed the layout so coordinates, solar angles, Earth visibility, and mission pins are all visible at once without cluttering the view.
